Opens, Shorts, Fuses, and Circuit Breakers

Unit 3: Electricity and Electronics. Lesson 14 of 53 in BMET Academy.

Nearly every electrical failure is one of two things: a path that should be complete and is not, or a path that exists where it should not. Learn how each one looks on a meter and you can diagnose a dead device without a manual.

The open circuit

An open is a break: a blown fuse, a switch that will not close, a wire broken inside its insulation, a cold solder joint, a corroded connector pin, a burned-out lamp.

  • Resistance across the break is infinite, and the meter shows OL.
  • No current flows anywhere in that loop.
  • With the power on, the full source voltage appears across the open, because no other part has current through it to drop any voltage.

That last point is the one that finds the fault. In a dead loop, put the probes across each part in turn. The part showing the whole supply voltage is the open one. A resistor with 0 V across it is innocent; it simply has no current.

The short circuit

A short is an unintended path of almost no resistance: a solder bridge, a pinched wire against a metal case, a screw dropped on a board, insulation worn through, liquid spilled inside.

  • Resistance is near zero, so continuity beeps.
  • Ohm's law then asks for an enormous current, because the denominator collapsed.
  • The result is heat: a hot wire, a burned trace, scorched plastic, smoke, fire, and a fuse or breaker opening if the circuit is protected.

A short across a part shows no voltage across that part even with the power on, because a near-zero resistance cannot develop a voltage.

Finding each one

Fault   Ohms (power off)   Continuity   Volts across it (power on)
open    OL                 silent       the full source voltage
short   near 0 ohm         beeps        about 0 V
good    its rated value    silent       its normal share of the supply

Work with the power off for ohms and continuity, and isolate at least one end of the part so other parts in parallel do not fool you.

Fuses

A fuse is a deliberate weak link in series with the circuit. Its thin element melts and opens before the wiring, the board, or the transformer is damaged.

  • Every fuse carries a current rating and a voltage rating, and both must match the original.
  • Fast-acting fuses open almost at once and protect sensitive electronics. Slow-blow (time-delay) fuses tolerate a brief inrush, which is what a motor or a transformer draws the instant it is switched on. Fitting a fast fuse where a slow one belongs gives you a device that blows a fuse every time it starts.
  • Never replace a fuse with a larger one and never bypass one with a jumper or foil. The fuse is the only thing standing between a fault and a fire.
  • Find the cause first. A fuse opens for a reason. Clear the short, then fit a new fuse of the same rating, then power up. Replacing the fuse first just destroys the new fuse and teaches you nothing.

Circuit breakers and GFCI

A circuit breaker does the same job as a fuse but resets instead of being replaced; inside, a magnetic or heat-operated mechanism trips the contacts open. A breaker that will not stay set is reporting a fault, not failing.

A GFCI protects people rather than wiring. It compares the current going out on the hot conductor with the current coming back on the neutral, and if the two differ, the missing current is leaking somewhere it should not be, possibly through a person. It opens at an imbalance of 4 to 6 mA under the NFPA 99 requirement for wet locations, far below the current that could stop a heart. That is why a GFCI protects sinks, tubs, and therapy pools, and why its monthly test button matters.

In the lab you meet a dead loop with one open part and one shorted part, and the readings tell you which is which before you touch a tool.

Exam tip: open means OL on ohms and full voltage across the gap. Short means near 0 ohm, a beep, and no voltage across it. A fuse that blows again immediately means the short is still there.
Remember
Open: infinite resistance, OL, no current, full source voltage across the break. Short: near 0 ohm, beeps, huge current, heat and fire, and no voltage across the shorted part. Ohms and continuity with the power off. Fuses match current and voltage rating, fast or slow-blow, never bypassed, and you find the cause before fitting a new one. Breakers reset. A GFCI compares hot against neutral and opens at 4 to 6 mA under NFPA 99 for wet locations.

Deeper explanation

Opens, Shorts, Fuses, and Circuit Breakers, explained slowly

Two faults, mirror images

Every electrical failure reduces to a path problem. Either a path that should exist does not, or a path exists that should not.

                     Open                           Short
what it is           a break in the path            an unintended low-resistance path
resistance           infinite: the meter shows OL   near zero: continuity beeps
current              none in that loop              far more than intended
voltage across it    the full source voltage        about 0 V
heat                 none                           a lot: hot wires, burned traces, smoke
typical causes       blown fuse, broken wire,       solder bridge, pinched wire on the chassis,
                     cold joint, corroded pin,      dropped screw, worn insulation,
                     open switch, burnt-out lamp    liquid spill
how you find it      volts across parts, powered;   continuity, unpowered, one end isolated
                     ohms, unpowered

The voltage rule is the one that does the work. In a dead series loop, no current flows, so no good part can drop any voltage. Probe across each part in turn and the one showing the entire supply is the break. A resistor reading 0 V in a dead circuit is not faulty; it is simply idle.

A worked diagnosis

The lab circuit is a battery, a fuse, a closed switch, and two 1k resistors in a loop, and the device is dead.

  1. Across the fuse: 9 V. That is the whole supply, so the fuse is open.
  2. Across R1: 0 V. No current, so no drop. R1 is not the fault.
  3. Power off, ohms across the fuse: OL. Confirmed open.
  4. Power off, continuity across each part: R2 beeps and reads about 0.3 ohm. A 1k resistor should read about 1,000 ohm and stay silent, so R2 has a short across it.
  5. Conclusion: the short across R2 drew enough current to open the fuse.

The fix follows from the diagnosis, and the order matters: remove the short, then fit a new fuse of the same rating, then power up. Fitting the fuse first destroys the new fuse. Bypassing the fuse to "see if the rest works" removes the only protection in the circuit and can turn a cheap repair into a fire.

Fuses, properly

Property           What it means                         Rule
current rating     the amps it will carry indefinitely   replace with the same value, never larger
voltage rating     the voltage it can safely interrupt   same rating as the original, never lower
fast-acting        opens almost at once                  protects semiconductors
slow-blow          tolerates a brief inrush              motors, transformers, heaters
physical size      the body dimensions, as in 5 x 20 mm  it must fit the holder properly

A higher voltage rating is also safe, but match the original unless the manual says otherwise. A fast fuse fitted where a slow one belongs blows every time the device starts, because the inrush when a motor or transformer energizes is many times the running current. That is a repeatable, maddening fault whose cause is a parts-bin substitution.

Breakers and GFCI

A circuit breaker interrupts the same way a fuse does but resets, using a heat-operated strip for slow overloads and a magnetic element for sudden ones. A breaker that will not stay set is reporting a fault that is still present; holding it in is never the answer.

A GFCI protects people, not wiring. It continuously compares the current leaving on the hot conductor with the current returning on the neutral. Equal means all the current came back through the intended path. A difference means some of it went somewhere else, possibly through a person, and the device opens at an imbalance of 4 to 6 mA under the NFPA 99 requirement for wet locations. Compare that with the body-current table: 4 to 6 mA is around the accepted harmless level and far below the 100 to 300 mA that causes fibrillation. A GFCI is designed to open while the shock is still only unpleasant.
